newsitem.title: CANADA: BC Hydro sees no major problems from snow melt.
newsitem.headline: BC Hydro sees no major problems from snow melt.

text.p: BC Hydro, Canada's third-largest electric utility, expects no major operational problems from the melting of large amounts of snow in the southeast portion of British Columbia, a company official said.

"Given the B.C. system as a whole, we're not really in any unusual high or low supply situation," BC Hydro manager for generation planning Brian Fast said. "We've had ideal storage to handle the snow melt."
One exception was high water from snow melt on the Pend Orielle river system, which originates in the United States, flows north into southern B.C., then back into the U.S.

"The hydroelectric projects in the United States operated by BPA (Bonneville Power Authority) and the Corps of Engineers have been releasing a significant amount of water and that's been running through Canada," Fast said.
"At the moment, that's the only hydroelectric system of reservoirs that we're watching closely."
A spokewoman for Powerex, BC Hydro's marketing subsidiary, said export and import activity had not been hampered by snow melt and high reservoirs.
"We've been meeting our longer-term trades and we've been active in the shorter-term market," the spokewoman said. "We have of late been buying some off-peak energy."
Powerex has recently been able to purchase the light-load power at a lower cost for to store and sell at a later date, he said.
British Columbia government-owned BC Hydro has total generating capacity of 10,851 Megawatts including 9,716 Megawatts of hydroelectric generation.
Besides being active in the U.S. power market, the company also trades with Alberta utilities.
